title: Straw and plastic mulch effects on soil moisture retention in rain-fed sorghum: a two-season field trial

headings.text: Straw and plastic mulch effects on soil moisture retention in rain-fed sorghum: a two-season field trial

key_sentences: Soil water shortage during grain filling is the main constraint on sorghum yield in semi-arid smallholder systems.
We compared bare soil with straw mulch and black polyethylene film over two rainy seasons on a sandy loam.
Both mulches raised volumetric water content in the top 30 cm by 4.6 to 6.3 percentage points and increased grain yield by 36 to 57 per cent.
Rain-fed sorghum is grown on more than two million hectares of semi-arid land in the region, mostly by farmers with less than two hectares.
Three treatments were laid out in a randomised complete block design with four replicates.
Seasonal rainfall was 584 mm in 2025 and 471 mm in 2026, and the second season included a dry spell of 23 days at flowering.
Across both seasons, mulched plots held between 4.6 and 6.3 percentage points more water in the top 30 cm than bare plots.
Relative to the control, straw mulch increased yield by 36% in 2025 and by 51% in the drier 2026 season.
The larger relative gain in the drier season suggests that mulching is most valuable precisely when water is scarcest.
Straw mulch at 5 t ha⁻¹ is a low-cost way to conserve soil water and raise sorghum yields on sandy soils in semi-arid conditions.
